title: The IPG India Report
text:
## The IPG India Report

India is now the world’s most populous country, having overtaken China in 2023. It has also become the fourth largest economy, with a fast-growing confidence on the world stage and an ability to leverage its massive economic potential in a way that it has never done before. Recent trade deals with the European Union and an interim trade agreement with the US highlight India’s status as an increasingly attractive manufacturing partner for industries which had become over-dependent on China. At the same time, India is trying to stay friendly with Russia and gently attempting to improve links with China, with whom it shares a 2,000-mile border. Relations with Pakistan, however, are close to an all-time low with virtually no trade and extreme mutual suspicion between the two countries. Closer to home, a new bilateral trade agreement between India and the UK came into effect in July 2026. It eliminates or reduces tariffs and duties on 90% of UK products entering India. This report has been compiled by Jonathan Atkins, one of publishing’s most experienced export leaders. Jonathan recently retired from his position as international director at Pan Macmillan after a 40-year career in publishing that also included time at Penguin and Simon & Schuster. He managed Pan Macmillan India and Pan Macmillan South Africa and led his team to the British Book Award for Export in 2020. Export sales have always been his focus, but he has also been responsible for UK sales, foreign rights, audio publishing and third-party distribution.

This, combined with a more sophisticated and efficient retail infrastructure, suggests that India will continue to offer growth opportunities which are lacking in most of the more mature markets around the world. India’s cultural confidence is also booming, with cricket—India’s secular and unifying religion—and the Bollywood movie industry acting as major commercial drivers of the wider economy. Meanwhile, it’s hard to overestimate the importance of sacred religion to daily public and private life in India. For those of Hindu faith, by far the most dominant form of worship, and of the many other faiths including Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism and Jainism, religious festivals such as Diwali, Eid and even Christmas are hugely significant cultural and commercial events.

India is the fifth largest publishing market in the world, and the second largest for publishing in the English language behind the US. It is also without doubt the market with the greatest growth potential. While numbers are hard to verify, India’s market has an estimated value of $10 billion and has achieved double-digit growth in each of the last five years. NielsenIQ predicts the market will double in size by 2031, with the journals sector growing even faster. With 1.5 million schools and more than 1,200 universities, India’s market is massively driven by the education sector, which accounts for around 90% of sales. This sector

Amazon Kindle is the market leader for ebooks, but the uptake of reading devices has been limited, partly because they are so expensive. Kindle Unlimited is available, though with a restricted catalogue. Apple, Kobo and Google are all established in the market and offer digital audiobooks. Audible is the digital audio market leader with a monthly subscription fee of Rs199 (£1.54). Spotify hasn’t yet launched a digital audiobooks offering. Storytel was one

India has more than 22,000 book retailers. More than 60% of purchases are made online, with Amazon and Flipkart (80% owned by Walmart) the biggest players. Bookswagon.com is an important local platform that specialises in book products. Local marketplace sellers such as Amazing Buy, URead, Cocoblu and many more fulfil orders from these platforms. This is a consequence of India’s trade legislation, which restricts foreign companies from selling direct to consumers. Crossword is the biggest national chain of physical bookshops; it is based in Pune and is growing fast, with 120 stores in 40 cities.

All major international publishing groups have a presence in India and are mostly based in Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) including Noida and Gurgaon. Penguin Random House and HarperCollins have traditionally dominated third-party sales and distribution services for independent UK and US publishers. They all publish locally and some also acquire English language rights from agents and international publishers. There are around 9,000 active Indian publishers with many more small family-run presses. Around 90% are dedicated to educational publishing but there are growing numbers of smart and agile local trade

Half (50%) of trade sales are from non-fiction. Children’s and Young Adult have a 26% share and fiction 24%, and these are the fastest-growing trade sectors. Print dominates trade sales in India. It generates 95% of sales while ebook and digital audio formats are worth only 5%. Backlist titles accountfor 85% of all sales, rising to 94% in the children’s market. Overdrive is the leading digital delivery platform for institutional and library sales. Local platforms include eBookstore India (academic ebooks), Pratilipi, PenAStory (local self-published digital content) and Kuku FM (themarket-leading and fast-growing local audio platform).

Regional chains include Starmark (Kolkata), Bahrisons (Delhi), Higginbothams (Chennai), Om Books (Delhi), Sapna Book House (Bangalore) and Oxford Bookstores. Wholesalers include India Book Distributors and Prakash Books, which have regional sub-offices in most major cities. They supply virtually all retailers, online and offline, including chains, independents and the ‘informal’ book trade. The latest Indian retail initiative is ‘quick commerce’. New retail players like Blinkit are aiming to become the Deliveroo of books, offering the delivery of bestsellers to metro addresses in 10 minutes or less.

Penguin Random House is a long-established trade publisher in India, having opened in 1987. It has comfortably the biggest market share and publishes locally in all categories. HarperCollins has the second largest market share and is a major local publisher. It has a growing education division. Hachette launched in India in 2008. Its main focus is on the group’s lists. It has some distribution clients and a ‘boutique’ style local publishing programme. Pan Macmillan has operated in India in some form since 1892. Its education division still employs more than 500 people across 26 offices. Pan Macmillan India has grown considerably over the past five years and is now looking to offer third-party sales and distribution.

These publishers acquire English and local language rights. Manjul is particularly strong in self-help, health and wellbeing and spirituality. Its team are based in Bhopal and visit the Frankfurt and London Book Fairs, working closely with many international agents and publishers. Jaico is a long-established Mumbai based publishing and distribution company with a distinguished record of bringing under-represented international authors to prominence in India.

#### International publishers

#### Local publishers

Speaking Tiger is one of India’s most acclaimed independent publishing companies with adult and children’s books. It mostly publishes in English and attends the Frankfurt Book Fair in search of new and diverse voices. Prakash Books is a nationwide distributor that is branching out into local publishing. It has quickly become a leading children’s publisher under the Wonder House imprint. Fingerprint is its adult imprint. Juggernaut is a very innovative and dynamic publisher based in Delhi.

Bloomsbury has a strong non-fiction local publishing programme with authors including William Dalrymple and Shiv Khera, and a growing academic and professional profile. JK Rowling’s Harry Potter books give it a significant share of the children’s market. Simon & Schuster has some major US authors and client publishers including Viz Media. It recently announced a new distribution partnership with Penguin Random House. Scholastic has a big presence in the children’s market. It is almost entirely focused on its own content and locally created education resources for schools and book fairs.

Westland was acquired by Amazon in 2017, closed down in 2022, and has been publishing under new ownership since 2023. Rupa is a 90-year-old Indian trade publisher and distribution business that also publishes literary fiction and non-fiction under the Aleph imprint.

DC Books is based in Kerala and also owns a chain of bookstores and online retail platform. Om Books is a Delhi-based publisher and chain bookseller.

Pricing

This is a major challenge for all international publishers, and the main reason why such apparently high discounts are required by local distributors. Rs 499 (£3.88) is the most common price point for a UK mass-market fiction paperback title that has a Recommended Retail Price (RRP) of £9.99. Big, high-profile bestsellers might then be discounted by a further 25% to 35% by online retailers, which means the final selling price could be equivalent to 25% of the original UK cover price.
